## Fuzzy early warning systems for condition based maintenance

Nazanin Vafaei ⁎ , Rita A. Ribeiro, Luis M. Camarinha-Matos

UNINOVA and Faculty of Sciences and Technology, Nova University of Lisbon, 2829-516 Caparica, Portugal

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Fuzzy early warning system Decision support Maintenance Condition based maintenance

## 1. Introduction

Reducing production costs is a general goal of manufacturing firms and decreasing maintenance costs is one of their targets. In this sense, Wang, Chu, and Wu (2007) stated that 'maintenance plays an important role in keeping availability and reliability levels, product quality, and safety requirements'. Often, unnecessary or improper maintenance activities occupy up to one third of the total amount of maintenance budget in manufacturing firms (Mobley, 2002). Therefore, selecting appropriate maintenance strategies can contribute to increase production efficiency (Wang et al., 2007). Further, this study promotes building intelligent digital platforms to bridge the gap between industry/manufacturing and technology, since it is concerned with improving the quality of production in plants through more robust methodologies of maintenance.

In the literature, two types of maintenance strategies are usually considered: corrective and preventive (Li, Khoo, & Tor, 2006; Waeyenbergh & Pintelon, 2004). Corrective maintenance is applicable when a failure happens, while preventive maintenance is used before system failure, by doing systematic inspections and prevention of predicted failure (Wang, 2002). In the corrective maintenance strategy, actions are taken after the machines broke down and the production line cannot perform its planned tasks. On the other hand, preventive maintenance relies on periodic inspections, usually defined by experts based on their knowledge and experience from observing past events, to determine time intervals to do the inspection, especially for critical components and even replace them when needed (Elghazel et al., 2015). However, using preventive maintenance, regardless of the machine's condition, could be a disadvantage because the scheduled intervals for intervening are sometimes unnecessary since machines could

A B S T R A C T

Globalization and growing market competitiveness keep pressuring manufacturing firms to reduce costs and increase effectiveness, hence, improving condition based maintenance strategies may contribute to those aims. In this study we present a fuzzy early warning approach for improving pro-active Condition Based Maintenance (CBM) diagnostic strategies. The main objective is to provide early warnings on potential production line breakdowns or other hazardous situations, enabling more informed decisions on maintenance strategies. To demonstrate the approach usefulness, an illustrative example of a car production line is discussed.

be in healthy condition. Therefore, it may just cause avoidable extra costs, as for example, paralyzing operation to perform the maintenance (Elghazel et al., 2015). To counteract these situations, proposals for using condition based maintenance (CBM) appeared in the nineties and have been evolving according to new technological advances (Bousdekis, Magoutas, Apostolou, & Mentzas, 2015).

As mentioned by Bilge, Badurdeen, and Jawahir (2016), industries are increasingly improving effectiveness instead of efficiency, and industrial engineering and intelligent digital platforms helps manufacturing to achieve this goal. According to CBM strategies, maintenance decisions can be made on the basis of measured data from a set of sensors to support anticipation-driven sensing and proactive decision-making (Bousdekis et al., 2015). The data collected during any manufacturing process (historic data) can be used to determine when the equipment status is nominal, hence allowing maintenance staff to perform necessary actions before any potentially catastrophic damage occurs (Shafiee, 2015). Some CBM advantages are prior warnings of impending failures and increased precision in failure prediction. The main disadvantage are the costs of installing and using monitoring equipment and to develop decision making systems to monitor production line problems (Kothamasu, Huang, & VerDuin, 2006).

Recently, advances in cyber-physical systems, with cheap sensors promote adopting early fault detection systems, in production lines, with the aim of reducing production costs and increase effectiveness (Shafiee, 2015). Further, using fuzzy early warning systems may improve future effective maintenance policies, while keeping productivity standards and ensuring safety for industries and manufacturing firms (D'Angelo et al., 2014). Early warning systems include three main tasks (D'Angelo et al., 2014): (i) detecting potential faults while monitoring a system, (ii) isolating faults by identifying the location and type of faults, and (iii) determining the severity (alarm level) of the faults. This paper proposes a general approach to CBM strategies, based on the mentioned work (D'Angelo et al., 2014), but including two novelties: (1) using available historical data to define, automatically, the warning levels; (2) the outputs levels are associated with potential actions to improve CBM strategies in manufacturing production lines.

In addition, this paper is an extension of the paper presented at the CIE conference (Vafaei, Ribeiro, & Camarinha-Matos, 2017) and its motivation derives from the lack, in the literature, of adaptive (fuzzy) early warning systems to improve pro-active decision making in CBM. Two main works are the starting point and motivation for this article. One recent work on contributions to improve CBM, proposed by Bousdekis et al. (2015), whom defined a conceptual framework to predict undesired events by using pro-active decision to develop the CBM, however, they did not implement it. The second work, by Kumar and Chaturvedi (2009) defined a fuzzy alarm system to predict manifested degradation of equipment's, but it was not specifically addressed for pro-active decision in CBM strategies.

In summary, this work is a first step to demonstrate the suitability of applying Fuzzy Early Warning Systems (FEWS) for supporting more informed decisions on CBM strategies, thus improving their effectiveness. FEWS provide information about health status of equipment's and potential hazardous situations (Ribeiro, 2006), with alarm levels within the range [0, 1], where zero means everything is functional/nominal; 1 means there is a serious break down; and intermediate alarm-levels provide the respective severity level of the problem. With these intermediate levels there is ample time to schedule appropriate maintenances and avoid break-downs in production lines.

The paper is organized as follows. In this introduction we presented the topic of the article and its objectives. Section 2 provides a brief overview of Condition Based Maintenance; and Section 3 introduces Fuzzy Inference Systems, which provide the background model for the early warning system. The proposed fuzzy approach is explained in detail in Section 4. Section 5 discusses the implementation and validation of the developed fuzzy warning system for a production line case study. Finally, Section 6 presents the conclusions.

## 2. Background on condition based maintenance

Condition based maintenance refers to actions for maintaining current and future health of manufacturing systems, which are defined by gathering data within condition monitoring (Jardine, Lin, & Banjevic, 2006). Lee, Ni, Djurdjanovic, Qiu, and Liao (2006) defined CBM as ' the main idea of CBM is to utilize the product degradation information extracted and identified from on-line sensing techniques to minimize the system downtime by balancing the risk of failure and achievable profits '. There are different categories of model-based CBM: knowledgebased; data-driven; and combination of them (Goh, Tjahjono, Baines, & Subramaniam, 2006; Venkatasubramanian, 2005). In this study we use a data-driven approach for monitoring production lines and suggest possible actions with a fuzzy early warning system.

Bousdekis et al. (2015) also argued that CBM include diagnostic and/or prognostic models to define the potential maintenance actions in order to support more informed decisions. The diagnostic phase is done based with real-time data obtained by monitoring and fault detection in the system, while the prognostic phase needs calculation or estimation of remaining useful life (RUL) of machines and equipment (Ahmad & Kamaruddin, 2012; Jardine et al., 2006; Venkatasubramanian, 2005). Here we only address the diagnostic phase, following the sentence of Ahmad and Kamaruddin (2012) ' The main aim of diagnosis is to provide early warning signs to engineers while the monitored equipment is operating '. From the works just mentioned (Ahmad & Kamaruddin, 2012; Jardine et al., 2006; Venkatasubramanian, 2005), and (Bousdekis et al., 2015), we can state that early warning systems seem a good approach to support stakeholders to make proactive decisions by recommending appropriate maintenance strategies, define/propose actions and different maintenance schedules.

Furthermore, with progresses in cyber-physical systems and cheap sensors, it is increasingly easier: to collect data from many different sources; to monitor production processes; and provide early warning information for improving CBM in production lines. Early warning systems support detecting where a problem is emerging, which is the intensity of faults, and for how long the system can work with this potential fault in the production line (Tsang, Yeung, Jardine, & Leung, 2013). Tsang et al. (2013) believe that CBM is a good maintenance strategy when: (a) time-directed preventive maintenance is not applicable because faults happen randomly in the system, (b) a measurable parameter associated with the onset of failure can be recognized, and (c) the intervals and threshold can be defined for the parameters.

In recent studies, it is noticeable the increasing usage of computational intelligence techniques for monitoring and forecasting components' faults. For example, Bonissone and Goebel (2001) proposed the usage of fuzzy logic combined with neural networks and decision trees for anticipating (prognosis) break-downs in a paper mill. Grantner et al. (2010) used a FEWS to diagnose axle fatigue in Intelligent Vehicle Health Management System (IVHMS). Their model decreases the cost of maintenance and increases the vehicle availability by diagnosing the axle fatigue and predicting the remaining life of the axle based on CBM strategy (Grantner et al., 2010). Modification and adjusting of membership function and fuzzy rules are done with cluster extraction and reclustering operations (Grantner et al., 2010). Yang, Ma, and Zhao (2017) discussed the implementation of CBM to prevent failures that are caused by internal-based degradation and external fatal shocks in complex industries. Their proposed CBM policy uses normal thresholds and defective thresholds, besides the periodic inspections to decrease maintenance costs caused by degradation failures (Yang et al., 2017). In another study, Zhao, He, He, and Xie (2018) studied minimization of the expected cost rate in the CBM policy which has random delay time in the maintenance operations. Their maintenance strategy includes continuously monitoring and determination of cost rates depending on shock and degradation risks. They also discussed choosing more appropriate alarm thresholds to reach minimum expected cost rates. Ahmad and Kamaruddin (2012) compared time-based maintenance (TBM) and condition-based maintenance (CBM) regarding the characteristics of data required and collection, data analysis/modeling, and decision processes. They stated that CBM is more useful and realistic than TBM in those characteristics. Furthermore, they pointed there are many challenges for maintenance decision making and suggested more research is needed. So, our study will complement the work of Ahmad and Kamaruddin (2012) by proposing developing maintenance decision making strategies using FEWS.

There are other interesting works on maintenance strategies using other computational intelligence techniques. For example, using neural networks to solve problems in conducting prognostics of a centrifugal pump case (Lee et al., 2006). Also, De Boer and Klingenberg (2008) used a neural network in CBM to monitor vibrations. There are many other works using different CI techniques, such as (D'Angelo et al., 2014; Hussain, 2015; Jamshidi, Rahimi, Ait-kadi, & Ruiz, 2015; Kothamasu & Huang, 2007; Kumar & Chaturvedi, 2009; Shafiee, 2015; Wang et al., 2007), however, since their approaches are quite different from our proposed FEWS we will not discuss them any further.

## 3. Background on fuzzy inference systems for early warning

There are several studies introducing different classes of strategies for warning systems and fault isolation. Venkatasubramanian, Rengaswamy, Yin, and Kavuri (2003) divided these strategies in two classes: quantitative and qualitative strategies. For quantitative strategies, mathematical models are defined using domain knowledge, while for qualitative strategies pattern analysis is performed using historic process data (D'Angelo et al., 2014). Regarding qualitative approaches, several papers introduce different methods. In this work we follow a quantitative approach (but based on historical data) to define a fuzzy early warning system, with the aim of improving CBM strategies.

Classical inference systems can be defined as computerized systems that use knowledge and information from human experts on a specific domain and then capture that expertise in software (Ribeiro, 2006). Fuzzy inference systems (the basis of our fuzzy early warning system (FEWS)) are extended versions of classical inference systems that add fuzzy logic concepts (Mendel, 2001; Pedrycz & Gomide, 1998; Ross, 2004) to represent imprecise and approximate data and knowledge. There are several studies describing early warning systems and fault identification systems using computational intelligence techniques, e.g. fuzzy logic, neural networks, etc. (see for example (Kocyigit, 2015; Merabet, Bahi, & Halem, 2015; Ribeiro, 2006)). An important recent study about the importance of robust decision making in maintenance strategies, was presented by Chandrahas, Kumar Mishra, and Mahapatra (2014); however, they used a multi-criteria approach instead of an early warning system like us.

The most important concepts of fuzzy inference systems are fuzzy rules and linguistic variables. A fuzzy rule is defined as 'IF < fuzzy proposition > THEN < fuzzy proposition > ' (Pedrycz & Gomide, 1998; Ribeiro, 2006; Ross, 2004). Examples of atomic or compound propositions are: 'x is warm' (atomic) and 'x is warm and y is hot' (compound), where warm and hot could be terms of a linguistic variable 'temperature'. We can define a linguistic variable by a 3-tuple (X, N, U) where: X is the name of the linguistic variable; N includes the terms of that linguistic variable, i.e. membership functions that X can have; U defines the physical domain for the linguistic variable X. For the interested reader, there are many references on FIS (Fuzzy Inference Systems) explaining other details, as for example (Mendel, 2001; Ross, 2004).

FIS performs inference using implication operators (Ribeiro, 2006; Ross, 2004), being the most used the Mamdani implication and the Sugeno-Takagi one. The Mamdani operator is the most common one because of its self-explanatory characteristic and simplicity of calculation (Mendel, 2001; Ross, 2004). Mamdani implication requires the use of a defuzzification method (usually center-of-mass) to obtain a final crisp value (Ribeiro, 2006). The Sugeno-Takagi system does not need defuzzification because the aggregation is performed with the weighted average method, which directly provides a final crisp result.

The development of the proposed fuzzy early warning system (FEWS) includes three steps (adapted from (Mendel, 2001; Ribeiro, 2006; Ross, 2004)):

1. Fuzzification of the input variables using historical data to automatically construct the linguistic variables, i.e. the membership functions (demonstration in Section 4.1).
2. Definition of the rule-set using acquired knowledge from historic numerical data and expert knowledge (demonstration in Section 4.2).
3. Select the operators for the inference system, FEWS: (a) intersection and union operators for the firing level of the rule antecedent (here: min and max operators); (b) choose the implication operator for rules triggering (in our case we used Mamdani implication due to its explanatory capability); (c) choose the combination operator to aggregate all fired rules and obtain the final output membership function (here:max operator). In addition, chose the defuzzification method (here center-of-area was chosen) (demonstration in Section 5).

There are already some application of FEWS in the CBM field, as well as other approaches from the computational intelligence area, as described in Section 2 above (see for example (Bevilacqua, Braglia, Frosolini, & Montanari, 2013; Bonissone & Goebel, 2001; Bousdekis et al., 2015; Grantner et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2006)). However, none applies our automatic FEWS construction using historical data and also they do not use early-warnings for demonstrating how it could improve decision making on CBM strategies. Here we will not present more details about fuzzy early warning systems because they are discussed along the demonstrative example.

## Rational for using a fuzzy early warning systems (FEWS) for CBM improvement

The choice of using a fuzzy early warning system for CBM decision support is based on four characteristics (adapted from Ribeiro (2006)):

- It is difficult to define a general mathematical model for CBM strategies. In most production lines the factory's data does not provide a direct measure on how to assess the need for preventive maintenance on one machine. Rules and approximate reasoning are good candidates for supporting decision makers on these tasks.
- The complexity of parameters behavior is rather diverse. (a) The input data depends on parameters, such as machine, work experience and factory processes, i.e. it is not standard; (b) The variables data do not convey information about nominal or 'acceptable' behavior, therefore it is better to rely on statistics about past data behavior (Note: this logic is used in this paper to construct the membership functions).
- The variables boundaries are soft and not crisp. Usually, there are no reliable data or information about limits for 'good' scraping rate or 'good' effectiveness or 'acceptable' down time, i.e. the variables' limits are not precisely defined. Further, it is difficult to have access to knowledge (manufacturer restrictions or machine operators experience) about acceptable deviations on variables health status (e.g. machine X down time is not acceptable when higher than Y time-units).
- Decision-makers need support tools to make timely decisions and avoid costly situations. In our CBM case, the proposed FEWS aims at providing alarm-levels of different severity to help decision makers to take timely actions. This will certainly improve the CBM activity and reduce costs by avoiding breakdowns on production lines.

## 4. Demonstrative example of using FEWS for improving CBM in a production line machine

In this section, we describe an illustrative fuzzy early warning system (FEWS) for improving proactive decision making in CBM strategies. The illustrative dataset for the developed (FEWS) is a sample set from a real car parts manufacturing company (due to confidentiality issues the manufacturer and the car names are not disclosed here). The input (raw) data was extracted from the historical dataset, referring to six months of data production on a single machine. We applied some transformations and aggregations to obtain a simple and self-explanatory numerical dataset to demonstrate how a FEWS can improve CBM strategies. A sample of the historical data for 3 cars on 3 days is shown below (Fig. 1).

Our illustrative case includes four variables, chosen (from the historical data) for their potential to cause faults in a car production line: machine down-time (DT); Scrap-rate for regular cars (SC-R); Scrap-rate for premium cars (SC-P); and Overall Equipment In-efficiency (OEIE). It should be noticed that we performed a modification in the raw data to consider (in) efficiency (OEIE) instead of efficiency (OEE) as explained in the next paragraph. The rational for choosing those four variables was: (a) consultation/suggestions from a technical car expert (involved in the real car manufacturer project); (b) we believe the 4 variables are illustrative enough for discussing CBM decision strategies using a FEWS.

To build our input data-set we started by aggregating the historical data of all types of machine malfunctions, measured in minutes of inactivity, into a single variable named Down Time (DT). Regarding scrap rate (measured as a percentage), due its diversity, depending on expensive or average cars, we grouped them in two variables: (a) scrap of premium cars (SC-P), because they have higher requirements of quality of production; and (b) scrap of regular cars (SC-R), for cars with less quality requirements. The last variable considered is the Overall Equipment In-Effectiveness (OEIE). Although the raw data refers to effectiveness of equipment quality, in this work we use ineffectiveness, because OEE (overall equipment effectiveness) is a benefit criterion (the higher the value the higher its membership value), while all other three variables are cost criteria (i.e. the lower the value the better is the membership value). Therefore, to maintain consistency on all four variables, we changed OEE into a cost criterion, by using a simple negation operator (OEIE = 1 - OEE). This modification ensures uniformity of logic in all variables representation, i.e. all four variables are represented as cost criteria.

Fig. 1. Illustrative data for 3-days and two variables: downtime (DT) and Equipment efficiency (OEE).

Summarizing, the four input criteria for our early warning system are: Down Time (DT) - measured in minutes; Scrap for Regular cars (SC-R) - measured as a percentage rate; Scrap for Premium cars (SC-P) - measured as a percentage rate; Overall Equipment In-Effectiveness (OEIE) - measured as a percentage.

## 4.1. Creating linguistic variables for the input and output variables

After choosing the four criteria and preparing their respective input data, we can now define the linguistic variables (Ross, 2004) - corresponds to step 1 of FEWS development, Section 3. For our demonstrator we believe it is enough to consider three warning types of hazards levels for each variable: Green, Yellow and Red situations. These three severity-levels represent the terms for each linguistic variable and are defined through membership functions, as depicted in Table 1. There are many different topologies for defining membership functions (Ross, 2004), but here we opted for simple trapezoidal membership functions - from which, triangular functions are one particular case - to define the linguistic variables terms. This morphology choice was made after a comparative study with Gaussian functions, which proved more difficult to express both the domain intervals as well as the overlaps between the membership functions for the three situations.

The membership's construction started by defining the membership's domain intervals for the four variables, by calculating their mean, minimum, maximum and standard deviation (downtime, scrap premium, scrap regular, OEIE). This method of constructing membership functions is based on the work of (Santos, Fonseca, Barata, Ribeiro, & Sousa, 2008). There are other ways of building membership functions such as clustering or using expert's information (Ross, 2004), but, in our case, since real data existed, we used common statistics (min, mean, std, and max) to define the membership functions limits. Based on these calculated statistical measures we then consider 3 elements for each linguistic variable, corresponding to warning levels: nominal situation

## FEWS OUTPUT: alarm severity-levels

After defining the membership functions for the three terms of each of the four linguistic input variables, we must now define the linguistic output variable, called alarm severity-level. Let us assume it is enough to have 4 levels of severity warnings and these are represented by uniform membership functions (Green, Yellow, Orange, and Red), as depicted in Fig. 4. The reason for using uniform membership functions is to ensure the severity intervals will have the same type of action for a certain range. Clarifying, Green area (severity level green) means that all input membership values are within acceptable nominal values and the production line does not need any immediate maintenance/attention (i.e. values fall within the memberships green warning levels of input variables); Red area alerts mean there are important problems in the production line, which request immediate attention; the Yellow area expresses that some attention or maybe preventive maintenance is required to avoid problems in the production line; and Orange area levels mean there are problems requiring some attention and maintenance. Notice that the severity level is also provided at the x-axis, and this is why we chose the uniform topology for output alarm-levels. Formalizing, the output variable 'Severity-level' is a linguistic variable with four uniform severity alarms membership functions, as depicted in Fig. 4(a); and Fig. 4(b) depicts the respective MATLAB implementation.

## 4.2. Constructing the rule set

In this step we describe how we construct the FEWS rule set for the production line machine example. To ensure coverage of the complete search space we must consider 4 linguistic variables, each with its 3 terms (membership functions), and their possible combinations (3 * 3 * 3 * 3), which would amount to 81 possible rules. This number of rules is obtained based on the multiplication rule of probability (for further information please see (Tucker, 1967)). However, since our case is a demonstrator for discussing suitability of FEWS for improving CBM strategies, we reduced the rule-set following the rationale that some outputs are similar for different inputs (redundant); and other rules are complementary (i.e. when combined provide better results). In summary, our logical reasoning for simplifying the example rule set (Table 6) is:

- I. The output result will be Green if both SC-R and SC-P are Green and the other 2 variables are either Green or Yellow.
- II. 2 Yellow inputs will result in a Yellow output, except when SC-R or SC-P are Yellow and then it is Orange;
- III. 2 Yellow inputs in SC-R and SC-P will result in a Red output;
- IV. 1 Red input in SC-R or SC-P will result in a Red output;
- V. 2 Red inputs for OEIE and DT will result in a Red output.

## 5. Validation

To implement the early warning system demonstrator, we used MATLAB fuzzy toolbox. Due to MATLAB limitations, rules can only be implemented using either 'And' or 'OR' in the rule premise/antecedent (e.g. rule 5 could not be implemented, as is, because it uses AND and OR in the same rule premise). Therefore, the 8 'logical' rules defined (Table 6) have been expanded into 29 rules in the MATLAB implementation. Fig. 5 displays the 29 rules used.

We performed three types of validation, each with several tests, to demonstrate our approach is suitable for supporting better informed decisions for CBM strategies. The first validation includes tests for triggering alarm-levels to assess if the rules are logically defined for setting different actions for CBM maintenance of each component (variable). For example, in validation (1.a) the output result is red - caused by a SC-R Red situation (i.e. high scrap rate for regular cars) - therefore, decision makers should take actions for immediate maintenance of machine components regarding SC-R. In the second validation we tested the limits of variables' memberships, to assess if the defined alarm levels make sense when the input variables endure violations on their limits. Also, this validation provides support for decision makers and experts to define specific actions under normal or faulted conditions in CBM strategies. The third validation is done by generating random numbers (simulation) and run the FEWS to assess the results obtained. This last test demonstrates the FEWS model behaves properly within all range of numbers for each variable.

We believe, that early warning and pinpointing of production line problems (i.e. severity-level for each variable), provide practical insights toward improving CBM strategies and actions in any production line. Being aware of early warnings about difficulties in any production line may reduce unnecessary maintenance costs and ensure continuous availability of equipment at accepted levels.

Notice that the recommended actions are illustrative and based on the authors' experience and literature works; for real cases implementation, those actions will need to be validated and tuned by factory experts .

## 6. Conclusion

This paper demonstrates that using a fuzzy early warning system (FEWS) for production line fault detection, can improve CBM strategies with the aim of reducing costs with sudden shutdowns, unscheduled down times or unexpected high scrap levels (percentage). Also, we discussed how a FEWS approach can contribute to better control production lines faults and set-up pro-active measures before problems occur. To illustrate the proposed approach, we implemented and discussed a demonstrator for a simple car's spare parts production line to highlight its suitability for improving CBM strategies.

We performed extensive validations and tests on the FEWS to assess its consistency and robustness. The validation and tests performed clearly show how a fuzzy early warning system (FEWS) may provide useful suggestions for improving CBM strategies on production lines. Further, the battery of test performed on validation 3 showed that FEWS could also act as a 'what-if' tool (simulations) for decision makers to set in place pro-active maintenance interventions in companies. Furthermore, it is easy to see how the proposed FEWS can be easily tuned, as for example changing the intervals with historical data from other production lines. Finally, we hope the findings of this study may prove useful for real industrial applications such as oil, gas, aviation, etc.

Summarizing, from the results obtained we may conclude that fuzzy early warning systems (FEWS) clearly contribute to improve CBM strategies, specifically when the knowledge about faulty conditions is imprecise and the complexity and non-linear behavior of a production line makes it difficult to be solved with classical mathematical models. As future work we plan to test the approach on real-life case studies to assess its generality as a CBM tool improvement.
